claim: Chess recall skill advantage is large on game positions and small but reliable on random positions; Chase and Simon's 'no effect' was a low-power null.
agent_test: Recall test: structured vs scrambled context; expect small gain from scrambled but kept items.
audit_note: Minor: Chase and Simon's 'no effect' is called a possible low-power null (Gobet and Simon 1996 pose it as an open question), not established; Sala and Gobet meta-analysis (r=.41, k=28) covers several domains, not chess only.

claim: Largest chunk size grows with skill on game positions (Gong et al. 2015: 4.56 vs 2.60 pieces for rated players vs non-players), while the number of chunks recalled does not correlate with chess rating in brief-presentation recall; evidence on whether Chase and Simon's 1973 claim of a fixed number of chunks holds across skill is mixed.
agent_test: Measure chunk size and count in agent notes by skill level of prompt/memory.
audit_note: Gong et al. 2015 confirm largest chunk size is larger for rated players and number of chunks does not correlate with rating, but that is consistent with, not a refutation of, a constant-chunk-count claim; the evidence note that Chase and Simon's own count rose with skill (N=3) conflicts with the 'size not count' framing and could not be confirmed in the 1973 text.
claim_before_audit: Chunk size (not chunk count) grows with skill; the 1973 'same number of chunks at all skills' claim is not supported.

claim: The 2 s pause criterion finds chunks whose pieces share chess relations (attack, defence, colour, type); Gobet and Simon (1998) report that latencies on a computer display closely match Chase and Simon's, and Gong et al. (2015), using a different repeated-recall method to define chunks, also found that within-chunk pieces share more chess relations and that inter-piece latency tracks relations.
agent_test: Cluster agent retrieval order by latency/relations and compare to a labelled relation set.
audit_note: Gong et al. 2015 used the repeated-recall technique as an alternative to the fixed-pause (latency) criterion, criticising the latter, and found within-chunk pieces have more chess relations and inter-piece latency tied to relations; this converges with but is not a replication of the 2 s criterion. The 1998 computer-display replication is supported only by its abstract (full text not retrievable).
claim_before_audit: The 2 s pause criterion finds chunks whose pieces share chess relations (attack, defence, colour, type); replicated with a computer display in 1998 and with repeated recall in 2015.

claim: A fixed 7-chunk short-term store is too small for expert recall; templates (big chunks with slots) are needed. Masters reach 16.8 pieces in the largest chunk.
agent_test: Compare flat chunk memory vs chunks-with-slots notes at equal tokens on multi-fact recall.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: CHREST simulations of chess recall (Smith, Lane and Gobet 2008; Lane, Gobet and Cheng 2001) support a visual STM capacity of about 3-4 chunks: simulated accuracy relative to its maximum rises from 0.914 at capacity 3 to 0.985 at capacity 4 (1 s exposure), with a good qualitative match to human recall data.
agent_test: Cap working notes at 3-4 chunk-units and compare to larger caps.
audit_note: In Smith, Lane and Gobet the 0.914 to 0.985 is CHREST accuracy as a proportion of its own maximum at 1 s exposure (capacity 3 to 4), not a fit to human data, and the paper only claims a good qualitative match to human data; Lane, Gobet and Cheng (2001) abstract gives the 3-4 chunk limit; both are CHREST group papers.
claim_before_audit: Visual STM capacity of about 3-4 chunks fits human and CHREST data best (fit 0.914 at 3 to 0.985 at 4 chunks).

claim: Chunk learning cost parameters (8 s per new chunk, 2 s familiarisation, ~250 ms slot fill, 50 ms STM encode) were fixed from EPAM and then predicted 1-60 s recall with no refit.
agent_test: Not testable directly on an LLM; use only as relative cost ordering (new chunk >> slot fill).

claim: Recall follows P=100-B*exp(-c(t-1)); skill raises both the 1 s starting level and the later rate; masters already near ceiling at 1 s on game positions. Constants re-checked against Table 1 (Masters' game-position fit is weak, r2=.35).
agent_test: Vary exposure length to the agent and fit the curve by capability tier.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Mirror-image and quadrant-swap tests show chunks are location-specific (piece plus square), which rejects Holding's 2,500-chunk SEEK estimate.
agent_test: Perturb layout/order of stored notes and measure retrieval loss; location-specific memory predicts a drop.
audit_note: Gobet and Simon 1996 do report mirror-image impairment, cite Saariluoma's quadrant swap, and reject Holding's estimate (postulated chunks < 2,500), but every listed source is from the Gobet/Lane CHREST group (Lane and Gobet 2011 is a defence with no new data) and a rival view (Linhares and Freitas) disputes pure location coding; they also allow a weaker 'both encodings' version.

claim: Required store size is a debated estimate (50,000 per Simon; 100,000; 300,000 nodes in the CHREST master-level net; 2,500 per Holding); none is directly measured.
agent_test: Count distinct reusable patterns the agent library needs before returns flatten.

claim: Searchless depth in the SEARCH model rises as a power function of net size (below 1 ply with no chunks, ~2.5 at 1,000, ~4 at 30,000, over 5 at 100,000). Human depth data: de Groot 4.8 (experts) and 5.3 (GM) plies; Charness 2.3/4.1/5.7 at Elo 1300/2000/GM. Still model-only; no LLM test.
agent_test: Compare agent search depth against size of retrieved pattern library.

claim: Trained novices follow power-law practice curves (largest chunk 39*N^.31 and 55*N^.23, N=2) and CHREST matches them with 4,772-5,811 chunks and ~107 templates.
agent_test: Track agent recall vs number of stored cases; fit a power law.

claim: Templates also explain multi-board recall limits of 4-5 boards at ~60%, with rare exceptions (9 boards after months of mnemonic training).
agent_test: Present k independent items sequentially; measure retention vs k with and without a cue index.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Chunking alone does not explain level-of-processing and semantic-orientation results; chunk access to semantic memory is needed. Independent Lane & Chang (2018, N=79): chess knowledge r=.67 with recall, 16% unique variance after experience; Gf adds 13%.
agent_test: Compare surface-index vs semantic-index retrieval.

claim: Random-material expert advantage generalises across domains: meta-analysis 24 studies, 28 samples, N=903, r=.41 [.29,.51]; publication-bias-adjusted r=.29 [.17,.41]; sports and 'other' domains have CIs crossing 0 (verified from full text).
agent_test: Cross-domain recall control for the agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: CHREST categorises chess openings at ~85% (French vs Sicilian), equal to an SVM; CogAct learns the same without hand-made features.
agent_test: Chunk-based retrieval vs embedding retrieval for pattern classification at equal tokens.

claim: Transformers trained on chess data win far less from a random start (16.7% vs 69.6%, 16-layer, 100,000-node Stockfish level 0); the 64% headline is the same model under time-limited Stockfish. 'Random board' = 20 random moves, an out-of-distribution start, not scrambled pieces.
agent_test: Run scrambled-vs-game recall on an LLM agent; the missing direct test.

claim: A 270M-parameter transformer that runs no explicit search at test time reaches a Lichess blitz Elo of 2895 against humans (Ruoss et al. 2024), but it was trained by supervised distillation of Stockfish 16 search-based action-values on positions from 10M games, so it shows that search results can be amortized into a pattern-matching network, not that patterns alone carry expert play.
agent_test: Compare retrieval-heavy vs search-heavy scaffold at equal tokens on a pattern-rich task.
audit_note: 2895 Lichess blitz Elo (270M, against humans) is verified, but the model is supervised distillation of Stockfish 16 search-derived action-values over 10M games' positions (15B annotations), not independent pattern recall; the authors call it an approximation of a search-based algorithm. Schultz et al. is another system (search-augmented MAV).
claim_before_audit: Searchless transformers reach Lichess blitz Elo 2895 (270M) by pattern recall from 10M games, so pattern stores can carry expert play without explicit search.

claim: Search added to a pretrained LLM raises strength further (MCTS 100 simulations: +68 internal Elo), so patterns and search are complements.
agent_test: Ablate retrieved patterns and search budget factorially.

claim: Replacing a finished subgoal trace with a summary chunk helps LLM agents: HiAgent raises GPT-4-turbo success from 21% to 42% with 35% less context; Context-Folding beats a summarise-when-full agent at the same 32K budget on BrowseComp-Plus (0.420 vs 0.386 prompt-only; 0.567 vs 0.527 with plain GRPO and 0.620 with its own FoldGRPO), with near-equal results on SWE-Bench Verified (0.492 vs 0.488 prompt-only); MEM1 (RL) uses about 27% of the peak tokens of Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct at 16 objectives (10.4 vs 38.4 hundred tokens).
agent_test: Re-run with summarise-on-subgoal-close at equal token budget on our tasks. b24 and c22 are the same paper.
audit_note: HiAgent (21 to 42, -35% context, GPT-4-turbo), Context-Folding prompt-only 0.420 vs 0.386 and MEM1 (10.4 vs 38.4 = 27%) verify, but 0.620 is the Folding agent trained with its own FoldGRPO versus 0.527 for a summary agent with plain GRPO; the like-for-like GRPO comparison is 0.567 vs 0.527, and on SWE-Bench Verified the RL summary agent (0.550) is about level with Folding GRPO (0.564).
claim_before_audit: Replacing a finished subgoal trace with a summary chunk helps LLM agents: HiAgent 21% to 42% success with -35% context (GPT-4-turbo); independent Context-Folding beats a summarise-when-full agent at equal 32K context (BrowseComp-Plus 0.420 vs 0.386 prompt-only; 0.620 vs 0.527 with RL); MEM1 (RL) cuts peak tokens to 27% of a 14B at 16 objectives. Prompt-only margin over other summarisers is small.

claim: Frontier LLMs degrade when board input is transformed: 180-degree rotation error 627 cp (Claude Sonnet 4.5) to 2531 cp (GPT-5.1) vs 195-181 cp for left-right mirror; location-specific knowledge as chunk theory predicts, with mirror tolerated (partial analogy).
agent_test: Rotate/reorder stored cases and check retrieval stability.

claim: LLM working memory shows an n-back limit like humans (d' about 1 at 3-back); chain-of-thought helps.
agent_test: Estimate agent n-back with and without scratchpad.

claim: No study found directly tests CHREST/EPAM constants or a De Groot structured-vs-shuffled recall on an LLM (gap search 2026-11-03 also found none); only indirect analogues (random-start chess, premise order, board rotation).
agent_test: Gap; run the test ourselves.

claim: LLM reasoning depends on the order of given facts: shuffling premises drops accuracy (12 rules: GPT-4-turbo 96.5% to 80.8%, PaLM 2-L 88.0% to 66.5%), gap growing with rule count; relevant items mid-context are retrieved worse than at the ends.
agent_test: Present the same fact set in solution order vs shuffled; keep active chunks at prompt start or end.
audit_note: Minor: 'shuffled' vs forward-order drop is for the logic benchmark with 12 rules; Lost in the Middle is a separate, well-known result for mid-context retrieval.

claim: Longer input hurts LLM reasoning well below the context limit: mean accuracy 0.92 at 250 tokens to 0.68 at 3000 (FLenQA); chain-of-thought does not remove the drop.
agent_test: Sweep working-set size in tokens and in chunk count; find the knee.

claim: Karvonen's 64% vs 69.6% win rates are the same 16-layer model under two Stockfish limits (time vs 100,000 nodes); not a contradiction.
agent_test: None; quote both with their engine setting.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Template theory has few independent tests: Lane & Chang (N=79) favour a conceptual-knowledge account alongside patterns; Saariluoma & Laine (N=2) fit curves but a frequency mechanism rivals CHREST; Gong et al. 2015 is the main recall replication.
agent_test: Hold both pattern notes and concept-level notes; test which retrieval gives more.

claim: Open, no evidence found: equal-token template (slot) notes vs flat notes; working-set cap in chunk units; library size at which gains flatten for an LLM; CHREST vs embedding retriever on classification at equal tokens; structured vs shuffled long-context recall on an LLM.
agent_test: Run these as our own ablations.
